answers.question: Analyze the circuit of Figure 13.

answer.text:
Figure 13 is an active-loaded **pMOS common-source stage**:

- \(M_2\) is the amplifying pMOS: source at \(V_{DD}\), gate at \(V_{in}\), drain at \(V_{out}\).
- \(M_1\) is a diode-connected pMOS load: its source is at \(V_{out}\), while its gate and drain are grounded. Thus it appears at the output as a two-terminal active load whose small-signal resistance is approximately
  \[
  R_{L,ac}\approx \frac{1}{g_{m1}}\parallel r_{o1}.
  \]

### Small-signal gain
Using the low-frequency small-signal model and including channel-length modulation,
\[
g_{ds i}=\frac{1}{r_{o i}},
\]
the voltage gain is
\[
\boxed{
A_v=\frac{v_{out}}{v_{in}}
=-\frac{g_{m2}}{g_{m1}+g_{ds1}+g_{ds2}}
}
\]
or equivalently,
\[
\boxed{
A_v=-g_{m2}\left(r_{o2}\parallel r_{o1}\parallel \frac{1}{g_{m1}}\right)
}
\]
The minus sign shows that the stage is inverting.

For \(g_m r_o\gg 1\),
\[
\boxed{
A_v\approx -\frac{g_{m2}}{g_{m1}}
}
\]
This is the “\(g_m/g_m\)” result: the load’s \(1/g_{m1}\) sets the gain.

If both transistors carry the same saturation current \(I_D\),
\[
g_{mi}=\sqrt{2\mu_p C_{ox}(W/L)_i I_D},
\]
so
\[
\boxed{
A_v\approx
-\sqrt{\frac{(W/L)_2}{(W/L)_1}}
}
\]
for identical pMOS process parameters. If \(M_1\) and \(M_2\) are identical and carry the same current, then \(A_v\approx -1\).

### Input and output resistance
At low frequencies the gate draws no current:
\[
\boxed{R_{in}\to \infty}
\]
The output resistance is
\[
\boxed{
R_{out}
=r_{o2}\parallel r_{o1}\parallel \frac{1}{g_{m1}}
\approx \frac{1}{g_{m1}}
}
\]
so the output is a relatively low-resistance node.

### DC operating point
In saturation, neglecting channel-length modulation,
\[
I_{D2}=I_{D1}
\]
gives
\[
\boxed{
V_{OUT,Q}
=
|V_{TP1}|
+
\sqrt{\frac{k_{p2}}{k_{p1}}}
\left(V_{DD}-V_{IN,Q}-|V_{TP2}|\right)
}
\]
where
\[
k_{pi}=\mu_p C_{ox}\left(\frac{W}{L}\right)_i.
\]

The amplifier is valid when
\[
V_{DD}-V_{IN,Q}>|V_{TP2}|
\]
so \(M_2\) is on, and \(M_2\) is in saturation for
\[
V_{OUT,Q}<V_{IN,Q}+|V_{TP2}|.
\]
The load \(M_1\) must be on:
\[
V_{OUT,Q}>|V_{TP1}|,
\]
and, once on, it is always in saturation because it is diode-connected.

If body effect is included, replace \(g_{m1}\) in the load conductance by \(g_{m1}+g_{mb1}\) (for the relevant bulk connection), giving approximately
\[
A_v\approx -\frac{g_{m2}}{g_{m1}+g_{mb1}}.
\]

Thus the circuit is an inverting pMOS common-source amplifier with a diode-connected pMOS active load. Its gain is set primarily by the transconductance ratio \(g_{m2}/g_{m1}\)—equivalently by the device aspect-ratio ratio—rather than by the bias current.

answer.text:
Assuming the two MOSFETs are enhancement PMOS devices (as indicated by the symbols), the circuit is a single-stage **PMOS common-source amplifier with a diode-connected PMOS active load**.  

- \(M_2\): input transistor; source at \(V_{DD}\), gate at \(V_{in}\), drain at \(V_{out}\).
- \(M_1\): load transistor. Its gate and drain are both at ground, while its source is at \(V_{out}\). Hence
  \[
  V_{SG1}=V_{SD1}=V_{out},
  \]
  so \(M_1\) is diode-connected and is in saturation whenever \(V_{out}>|V_{tp1}|\).

Let \(V_{tp1},V_{tp2}>0\) denote the magnitudes of the PMOS threshold voltages and let
\[
\beta_i=\mu_p C_{ox}\left(\frac{W}{L}\right)_i.
\]
Neglect body effect and channel-length modulation first.

### dc operating point
In saturation,
\[
I_{D2}=\frac{\beta_2}{2}\left(V_{DD}-V_{in}-V_{tp2}\right)^2,
\qquad
I_{D1}=\frac{\beta_1}{2}\left(V_{out}-V_{tp1}\right)^2 .
\]
At the output node, \(I_{D1}=I_{D2}\), giving
\[
\boxed{
V_{out}
=
V_{tp1}
+
\sqrt{\frac{\beta_2}{\beta_1}}
\left(V_{DD}-V_{in}-V_{tp2}\right)
}
\]
for the ideal square-law model with both devices saturated.  
With channel-length modulation included, solve instead
\[
\frac{\beta_2}{2}\left(V_{DD}-V_{in}-V_{tp2}\right)^2
\left[1+\lambda_2(V_{DD}-V_{out})\right]
=
\frac{\beta_1}{2}\left(V_{out}-V_{tp1}\right)^2
\left[1+\lambda_1 V_{out}\right].
\]
For a desired bias current \(I_Q\),
\[
V_{out,Q}=V_{tp1}+\sqrt{\frac{2I_Q}{\beta_1}},
\qquad
V_{in,Q}=V_{DD}-V_{tp2}-\sqrt{\frac{2I_Q}{\beta_2}}.
\]

The saturation conditions are
\[
V_{in}<V_{DD}-V_{tp2},
\qquad
V_{out}>V_{tp1},
\qquad
V_{out}<V_{in}+V_{tp2}.
\]
If \(V_{in}\) is too low, \(M_2\) enters triode; if too high, \(M_2\) cuts off and the circuit ceases to act as a linear amplifier.

### Small-signal voltage gain
Define
\[
g_{mi}=\sqrt{2\beta_i I_D}
\]
at the bias point, and \(r_{oi}=1/(\lambda_i I_D)\). The small-signal model gives
\[
\boxed{
R_{in}\approx \infty
}
\]
at low frequency, and
\[
\boxed{
R_{out}
=
r_{o2}\,\|\,r_{o1}\,\|\,\frac{1}{g_{m1}}
}
\]
(if body effect is significant in \(M_1\), replace \(g_{m1}\) by \(g_{m1}+g_{mb1}\)). Equivalently,
\[
\boxed{
A_v=\frac{v_{out}}{v_{in}}
=
-g_{m2}R_{out}
=
-\frac{g_{m2}}{g_{m1}+g_{ds1}+g_{ds2}}

\[
I_{D1}=I_{D2}=I_1 .

\[

\]
\[

\]

\[
V_{IN}>V_{T1},\qquad V_X\ge V_{IN}-V_{T1},
\]
and
\[

\]
\[
V_{out}\ge V_X+(V_{b1}-V_X-V_{T2})
       =V_{b1}-V_{T2}.
\]

\[

    =\frac12 k_{n2}(V_{b1}-V_X-V_{T2})^2,
\]
where \(k_{ni}=\mu_n C_{ox}(W/L)_i\). Thus
\[
V_{OV1}=\sqrt{\frac{2I_1}{k_{n1}}},\qquad
V_{OV2}=\sqrt{\frac{2I_1}{k_{n2}}},
\]
\[
V_{IN,Q}\simeq V_{T1}+V_{OV1},\qquad
V_X\simeq V_{b1}-V_{T2}-V_{OV2}.
\]

\[
V_X\ge V_{OV1},
\]

\[
g_{mi}=\frac{\partial I_{Di}}{\partial V_{GSi}}
      \approx \sqrt{2k_{ni}I_1}
      =\frac{2I_1}{V_{OVi}},
\]
\[
r_{oi}\approx \frac{1}{\lambda_i I_1}
\quad\text{(or }r_{oi}=\frac{V_{A,i}}{I_1}\text{)}.
\]

\[

\[

\[

r_{o2}\approx \frac{1}{\lambda_2 I_1}.

\[

=
-\frac{g_{m1}\left(g_{mT}+1/r_{o2}\right)}
{\displaystyle
\frac{1}{r_{o1}r_{o2}}
+
\frac{g_{mT}+1/r_{o1}+1/r_{o2}}{R_L}
}.
\]

\[

=
-\frac{g_{m1}\left(g_{mT}+1/r_{o2}\right)}

=
-g_{m1}r_{o1}\left[1+g_{mT}r_{o2}\right].
\]

\[

\[

=
r_{o1}+r_{o2}
+\left(g_{m2}+g_{mb2}\right)r_{o1}r_{o2}
\approx
\left(g_{m2}+g_{mb2}\right)r_{o1}r_{o2},

\[

\[

=

\[

=

\[

-g_{m1}\left[
r_{o1}+r_{o2}

\[

-g_{m1}\left(g_{m2}+g_{mb2}\right)r_{o1}r_{o2}.

\(g_{m2}, r_{o2}\) to \(M_2\), and

The same dc current flows through the stack:
\[
I_{D1}=I_{D2}=I_1.
\]
With
\[
V_{GS1}=V_{IN},\qquad V_{DS1}=V_X,
\]
\[
V_{GS2}=V_{b1}-V_X,\qquad V_{DS2}=V_{out}-V_X,
\]
the saturation conditions are approximately
\[
V_X \ge V_{IN}-V_{TH1},
\]
\[
V_{out}\ge V_X+(V_{b1}-V_X-V_{TH2})
      =V_{b1}-V_{TH2}.
\]
Equivalently, in terms of overdrives,
\[
V_X\ge V_{OV1},\qquad
V_{out}\ge V_X+V_{OV2}.
\]
For maximum output swing, \(M_2\) is biased so that
\[
V_{b1}\approx V_{TH2}+V_{OV1}+V_{OV2},
\]
giving a lower output compliance of about
\[
V_{out,\min}\approx V_{OV1}+V_{OV2}.
\]
The upper limit is set by the current-source load compliance, or approximately \(V_{DD}\) for an ideal source.

Using the square-law model, with \(K_i=\mu_n C_{ox}(W/L)_i\),
\[
I_1=\frac12 K_1(V_{IN}-V_{TH1})^2
\]
and

g_{m1}\simeq \frac{2I_1}{V_{OV1}}=\sqrt{2\mu_n C_{ox}(W/L)_1 I_1},
\qquad
g_{m2}\simeq \frac{2I_1}{V_{OV2}},
\]
\[
r_{o1}\simeq \frac{1}{\lambda_1 I_1},\qquad
r_{o2}\simeq \frac{1}{\lambda_2 I_1}.

\[

\]
Then the small-signal output resistance of the \(M_1\)-\(M_2\) cascode is
\[
R_{out}\simeq r_{o1}+r_{o2}+g_{me}r_{o1}r_{o2}
\approx g_{me}r_{o1}r_{o2}.
\]
The input resistance at the gate of \(M_1\) is ideally
\[
R_{in}\to\infty
\]
at low frequency.

The low-frequency voltage gain is, to good approximation,
\[

\approx -g_{m1}\,(R_{out}\parallel R_L),
\]
where \(R_L\) represents the finite output resistance of the current source and any external load to ac ground. For an ideal current-source load and no external load, \(R_L=\infty\), giving
\[

\[

\[

\qquad

answers.question: Explain why the Miller effect is less pronounced in a cascode.

answer.text:
The Miller effect is the multiplication of a feedback capacitance \(C_f\) between input and output when the stage has voltage gain. At the input it appears approximately as

\[
C_{\text{in,Miller}}\approx C_f(1-A_v),
\]

where \(A_v=V_{\rm out}/V_{\rm in}\). For an inverting amplifier, \(A_v<0\), so \(C_{\text{in}}\approx C_f(1+|A_v|)\). A large voltage gain therefore makes a small drain–gate or collector–base capacitance look much larger at the input.

In a simple common-source/common-emitter stage, the drain/collector drives a high-impedance load, so

\[
A_v\approx -g_m R_L
\]

and the gate–drain capacitance is multiplied by \(1+g_mR_L\). This can be a large Miller multiplication.

A cascode changes this. The input device’s drain/collector does not drive the output directly; it drives the source/emitter of a common-gate/common-base transistor whose gate/base is at ac ground. Looking into that node, the cascode transistor presents a low resistance:

\[
R_x \approx \frac{1}{g_{m2}+g_{mb2}}
\quad\text{(MOS)}
\qquad
R_x\approx r_{e2}
\quad\text{(BJT)}.
\]

Thus the input transistor’s local voltage gain to its own drain/collector is only about

\[
A_x\approx -g_{m1}R_x
\approx -\frac{g_{m1}}{g_{m2}+g_{mb2}},
\]

which is of order unity, rather than \(-g_mR_L\). Its small feedback capacitance \(C_{gd1}\) or \(C_{\mu1}\) therefore sees only a Miller factor of about

\[
1+|A_x|\sim 1\text{ to a few},
\]

instead of being multiplied by the full amplifier gain. The large output voltage swing occurs at the drain of the upper common-gate transistor. Since that transistor’s gate is at ac ground, its drain–gate capacitance goes from the output to ground, not from output back to the input, so it does not produce input Miller multiplication.

In short: the cascode transistor acts as a low-impedance current buffer/shield between the input transistor and the output. It prevents the input device’s drain from having a large voltage gain and prevents the output swing from being fed back to the input through the input transistor’s feedback capacitance. Hence the Miller effect is greatly reduced, increasing input bandwidth and reverse isolation.

This reduction is not perfect: finite output resistance, parasitic capacitance at the internal cascode node, and the finite impedance at the upper transistor’s gate (if not well bypassed) allow some Miller/feedthrough effects, especially at very high frequencies.

answer.text:
In a common-source/common-emitter stage, the gate–drain (or base–collector) capacitance \(C_{gd}\) bridges a high-gain inverting node, so the input sees an effective capacitance

\[
C_{\rm in}\approx C_{gs}+C_{gd}(1+|A_v|),
\]

where \(A_v\) is the stage voltage gain. A large gain makes \(C_{gd}\) look much larger—the Miller effect.

In a cascode, the input transistor’s drain is connected to the source/emitter of a common-gate/common-base transistor. That node has a low impedance, approximately

\[

\]

so the voltage gain of the input transistor is only

\[
|A_{v1}|\approx g_{m1}R_{\rm in,CG}\approx \frac{g_{m1}}{g_{m2}},
\]

typically of order unity. Thus the input transistor’s drain/collector voltage hardly swings compared with the overall output. Its \(C_{gd}\) is multiplied by only about \(1+g_{m1}/g_{m2}\), not by the full cascode gain.

The upper cascode transistor supplies the large output voltage swing, but its gate/base is at AC ground. Its drain–gate or collector–base capacitance therefore appears mainly from the output node to ground rather than as feedback from output back to the input.

So the cascode reduces the Miller effect because the low-impedance cascode node “shields” the input device from the large output swing, and the upper device isolates the high-gain output from the input. The effect is reduced, not completely eliminated; finite output resistance, device capacitances, and imperfect AC grounding of the cascode gate/base leave some residual Miller multiplication.

answers.question: Explain why the Miller effect is less pronounced in a cascode.

answer.text:
The Miller effect is greatly reduced in a cascode because the input transistor’s drain/collector does **not** swing with the full output voltage.

For a feedback capacitance \(C_f\) between an input and a node with voltage gain \(A_v\), the input sees

\[
C_{\rm in,eff}=C_f(1-A_v).
\]

In a simple common-source/common-emitter stage, \(C_{gd}\) or \(C_{bc}\) connects gate/base to drain/collector, and the drain/collector has a large inverted gain, \(A_v\approx -g_mR_D\). Thus \(C_{\rm in,eff}\approx C_f(1+|A_v|)\), which can be very large.

In a cascode, a common-gate/common-base transistor is inserted between the input device and the output. Looking into its source/emitter gives a low resistance:

\[
R_{\rm in,CG}\approx \frac{1}{g_{m2}}+\frac{R_L}{g_{m2}r_{o2}},
\]

usually close to \(1/g_{m2}\). Therefore the lower transistor’s drain/collector—the internal node—has only a small voltage gain, approximately

\[
A_x=\frac{v_x}{v_i}\approx -\frac{g_{m1}}{g_{m2}},
\]

which is about \(-1\) for equal transconductances. Hence the feedback capacitance of the input device is multiplied by only about

\[
1-A_x \approx 1+\frac{g_{m1}}{g_{m2}}\approx 2,
\]

rather than by the large overall output gain.

Equivalently, the upper common-gate/common-base device acts as a current buffer: it transfers the signal current to a high-impedance, high-swing output while keeping its input node at low impedance. Its own gate/base is ac-grounded, so its drain/collector-to-gate/base capacitance mostly loads the output and does not feed back to the overall input.

Thus the input capacitance of a cascode is much smaller and its input pole is pushed to a higher frequency. The Miller effect is not eliminated completely—finite transistor output resistance and high-frequency coupling through the upper device allow some feedback—but it is much less pronounced.

\[
V_{GS2}=V_{b1}-V_{\rm in}>V_{Tn},\qquad
V_{DS2}=V_{\rm out}-V_{\rm in}\ge V_{GS2}-V_{Tn}
\]

so

\[
V_{\rm out}\gtrsim V_{b1}-V_{Tn}.
\]

For the PMOS load,

\[
V_{SG1}=V_{DD}-V_{b2}>|V_{Tp}|,\qquad
V_{SD1}=V_{DD}-V_{\rm out}\ge V_{SG1}-|V_{Tp}|
\]

so

\[
V_{\rm out}\lesssim V_{b2}+|V_{Tp}|.
\]

Thus, for saturation,

\[
V_{b1}-V_{Tn}\;\lesssim\; V_{\rm out}\;\lesssim\; V_{b2}+|V_{Tp}|,
\]

with the threshold of \(M_2\) modified by body effect if its body is tied to ground rather than to its source.

At dc, there is no output load current, so the two drain currents must match:

\[
I_{D1}(V_{b2},V_{DD}-V_{\rm out})
=
I_{D2}(V_{b1}-V_{\rm in},V_{\rm out}-V_{\rm in}).
\]

Using the square law, for example,

\[
\begin{aligned}
I_{D2}&\simeq
\frac12\mu_n C_{ox}\left(\frac WL\right)_2
(V_{b1}-V_{\rm in}-V_{Tn})^2
\left[1+\lambda_n(V_{\rm out}-V_{\rm in})\right],\\
I_{D1}&\simeq
\frac12\mu_p C_{ox}\left(\frac WL\right)_1
(V_{DD}-V_{b2}-|V_{Tp}|)^2
\left[1+\lambda_p(V_{DD}-V_{\rm out})\right].
\end{aligned}
\]

These equal currents set the quiescent \(V_{\rm out}\) and \(I_Q\). If channel-length modulation is neglected, the dc output level is very sensitive to a current mismatch and is normally set by feedback or a following load.

\[
g_{o1}=\frac1{r_{o1}},\qquad
g_{o2}=\frac1{r_{o2}}.
\]

\[
v_{gs2}=-v_i,\qquad v_{bs2}=-v_i.
\]

At the output node, KCL gives

\[
-(g_{m2}+g_{mb2})v_i+
\frac{v_o-v_i}{r_{o2}}+
\frac{v_o}{r_{o1}}=0.
\]

Therefore the low-frequency voltage gain is

\[
\boxed{
A_v=\frac{v_o}{v_i}
=
\frac{g_{m2}+g_{mb2}+g_{o2}}
{g_{o2}+g_{o1}}
=
(g_{m2}+g_{mb2}+g_{o2})
\,(r_{o1}\parallel r_{o2})
}
\]

or, including an external output load \(R_L\),

\[
\boxed{
A_v
=
(g_{m2}+g_{mb2}+g_{o2})
\,(r_{o1}\parallel r_{o2}\parallel R_L).
}
\]

\[
A_v\approx (g_{m2}+g_{mb2})(r_{o1}\parallel r_{o2})
\approx g_{m2}(r_{o1}\parallel r_{o2})
\]

if body effect is neglected. If the PMOS load were an ideal current source, \(r_{o1}\to\infty\), and the gain would be limited by \(r_{o2}\).

\[
g_{mb2}
=
\frac{\gamma\,g_{m2}}{2\sqrt{2\phi_F+V_{SB}}},
\qquad V_{SB}=V_{\rm in}-V_{\rm body}.
\]

Looking into the source terminal at low frequency, with a total passive load \(R_D=r_{o1}\parallel R_L\) at the output,

\[
\boxed{
R_{\rm in}
=
\frac{r_{o2}+R_D}
{1+(g_{m2}+g_{mb2})r_{o2}}
}
\]

so to first order

\[
R_{\rm in}\approx \frac{1}{g_{m2}+g_{mb2}},
\]

\]

\[

=
r_{o1}\parallel R_L\parallel
\left[
r_{o2}+\left(1+(g_{m2}+g_{mb2})r_{o2}\right)R_s
\right].
}
\]

- \(M_1\): PMOS current-source active load.
- Output is in phase with the input: \(A_v>0\).

For the PMOS load in saturation,
\[
V_{SG1}=V_{DD}-V_{b2},\qquad
V_{SD1}=V_{DD}-V_{\rm out},
\]
\[
I_{D1}=\frac12 \mu_p C_{ox}\left(\frac WL\right)_1
(V_{DD}-V_{b2}-|V_{Tp}|)^2
\bigl[1+\lambda_p(V_{DD}-V_{\rm out})\bigr],
\]
with
\[
V_{DD}-V_{b2}>|V_{Tp}|,\qquad
V_{\rm out}<V_{b2}+|V_{Tp}|.
\]

The quiescent output is found by solving \(I_{D1}=I_{D2}\). Thus the usable output range is approximately
\[
V_{b1}-V_{Tn} < V_{\rm out} < V_{b2}+|V_{Tp}|,
\]
subject also to \(0<V_{\rm out}<V_{DD}\). If \(\lambda=0\), both currents are nearly independent of \(V_{\rm out}\); the bias voltages/sizes must be chosen so the currents match. In a real circuit the finite output resistances set \(V_{\rm out}\).

### 2. Small-signal behavior
At ac, both \(V_{b1}\) and \(V_{b2}\) are grounds. The PMOS load contributes only its output resistance \(r_{o1}\). For \(M_2\), define
\[
G_m=g_{m2}+g_{mb2},
\]
where \(g_{mb2}=0\) if the body is tied to the source; if the body is grounded, the body-effect term is included. Let
\[
R_L=r_{o1}\parallel R_{L,\rm ext},
\]
with \(R_{L,\rm ext}\to\infty\) if no external load is connected.

For an ideal voltage source directly driving \(V_{\rm in}\),
\[
\boxed{
A_v=\frac{v_{\rm out}}{v_{\rm in}}
=
\left(G_m+\frac{1}{r_{o2}}\right)(R_L\parallel r_{o2})
=
\frac{\bigl[1+G_m r_{o2}\bigr]R_L}{r_{o2}+R_L}
>0
}
\]
so the stage is **non-inverting** from source input to drain output. In the usual approximation \(G_m r_{o2}\gg1\),
\[
\boxed{A_v\approx G_m(R_L\parallel r_{o2})}
\]
or, with no external load,
\[
\boxed{A_v\approx (g_{m2}+g_{mb2})(r_{o1}\parallel r_{o2}).}
\]
If the body effect and \(M_2\) output resistance are neglected, this reduces to the familiar result
\[
A_v\approx g_{m2}r_{o1}.
\]

The small-signal input resistance at the source is
\[
\boxed{
R_{\rm in}=\frac{v_{\rm in}}{i_{\rm in}}
=\frac{r_{o2}+R_L}{1+G_m r_{o2}}
\approx \frac{1}{g_{m2}+g_{mb2}}.
}
\]
This is the characteristic **low input resistance** of a common-gate stage.

With the input voltage source set to zero (ideal source, source terminal ac-grounded), the output resistance is
\[
\boxed{
R_{\rm out}=r_{o1}\parallel r_{o2}
}
\]
(parallel with any external load). If the driving source has a finite source resistance \(R_s\), the resistance looking into the drain of \(M_2\) becomes
\[
R_{\rm out,M2}
=r_{o2}\bigl[1+(g_{m2}+g_{mb2})R_s\bigr]+R_s,
\]
so
\[
R_{\rm out}=r_{o1}\parallel R_{\rm out,M2}.
\]
For a source generator with resistance \(R_s\), the overall voltage gain is reduced by the input divider:
\[
\frac{v_{\rm out}}{v_{\rm sig}}
=
\frac{R_L}{R_s+R_{\rm in}}
\]
when \(v_{\rm sig}\) is the ideal generator voltage behind \(R_s\).

### 3. Circuit interpretation
- \(M_2\) converts the input voltage at its source into a signal current.
- \(M_1\) supplies an approximately constant bias current and presents a high resistance at the output, giving high voltage gain.
- The stage has **low input resistance, high output resistance, and non-inverting voltage gain**; it is often used as a current buffer or in cascode/RF input stages.
- Numerical values of \(V_{\rm out}\), gain, and resistances cannot be determined from the figure alone; they require \(V_{b1},V_{b2},V_{DD},\) transistor sizes, and process parameters.

Setting \(g_{mb2}=0\) gives the usual textbook result when the body effect is neglected.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in Figure 17.

answer.text:
**Circuit identification.**  
Figure 17 is a single-ended **common-gate NMOS amplifier with a PMOS current-source load**:

- \(M_2\): NMOS common-gate device. Its gate is held at \(V_{b1}\) (ac ground), its source is the input \(V_{\rm in}\), and its drain is the output \(V_{\rm out}\).
- \(M_1\): PMOS current-source load. Its source is at \(V_{DD}\), its gate is biased at \(V_{b2}\) (ac ground), and its drain is connected to \(V_{\rm out}\).

Thus the signal enters the source of \(M_2\), and the output is taken at the drain. The PMOS load provides a high small-signal resistance so that a large voltage gain can be obtained.

---

### DC bias and saturation

Let the dc value of the input be \(V_{IN}\), and let  
\[
V_{OV2}=V_{B1}-V_{IN}-V_{TN}>0
\]
be the overdrive of \(M_2\), and
\[
V_{OV1}=V_{DD}-V_{B2}-|V_{TP}|>0
\]
be the overdrive magnitude of the PMOS load.

For \(M_2\) to remain in saturation,
\[
V_{DS2}=V_{OUT}-V_{IN}\ge V_{OV2},
\]
and for \(M_1\) to remain saturated,
\[
V_{SD1}=V_{DD}-V_{OUT}\ge V_{OV1}.
\]
Equivalently,
\[
V_{B1}-V_{TN}\le V_{OUT}\le V_{B2}+|V_{TP}|,
\]
with \(V_{B1}>V_{IN}+V_{TN}\) and \(V_{B2}<V_{DD}-|V_{TP}|\).

The quiescent current is set by matching the two device currents:
\[
I_Q=I_{D2}=I_{D1}.
\]
Neglecting channel-length modulation initially,
\[
I_Q\simeq \frac12 \mu_n C_{ox}\left(\frac{W}{L}\right)_2
(V_{B1}-V_{IN}-V_{TN})^2
\]
and
\[
I_Q\simeq \frac12 \mu_p C_{ox}\left(\frac{W}{L}\right)_1
(V_{DD}-V_{B2}-|V_{TP}|)^2.
\]
Including \(\lambda\),
\[
I_Q=
\frac12 k_n'(W/L)_2 V_{OV2}^2
\left[1+\lambda_n(V_{OUT}-V_{IN})\right]
=
\frac12 k_p'(W/L)_1 V_{OV1}^2
\left[1+\lambda_p(V_{DD}-V_{OUT})\right],
\]
which determines the quiescent \(V_{OUT}\). In many textbook analyses, ideal bias current sources are assumed and \(V_{OUT}\) is chosen inside the saturation range above.

---

### Small-signal model

Both gates are at ac ground. The PMOS load therefore appears at the output as its small-signal output resistance
\[
r_{o1}=\frac{1}{\lambda_p I_Q},
\]
and \(M_2\) has
\[
g_{m2}=\frac{2I_Q}{V_{OV2}}
\]
and
\[
r_{o2}=\frac{1}{\lambda_n I_Q}.
\]
If the bulk of \(M_2\) is not tied to its source, include the body-effect transconductance \(g_{mb2}\); otherwise set \(g_{mb2}=0\). Define
\[
G_m=g_{m2}+g_{mb2}.
\]

Applying KCL at the output gives
\[
\frac{v_{out}}{v_{in}}
=
\frac{G_m+\frac{1}{r_{o2}}}
{\frac{1}{r_{o1}}+\frac{1}{r_{o2}}}
=
\left(G_m+\frac{1}{r_{o2}}\right)
\left(r_{o1}\parallel r_{o2}\right).
\]
Usually \(g_m r_o\gg 1\), so
\[
\boxed{
A_v=\frac{v_{out}}{v_{in}}
\approx (g_{m2}+g_{mb2})(r_{o1}\parallel r_{o2})
}
\]
or, if body effect is neglected,
\[
\boxed{A_v\approx g_{m2}(r_{o1}\parallel r_{o2})}.
\]

The gain is **positive/non-inverting** from \(V_{\rm in}\) to \(V_{\rm out}\): increasing the source voltage of \(M_2\) reduces its \(V_{GS}\), reducing its drain current and causing the output node to rise.

The small-signal output resistance is
\[
\boxed{
R_{out}\approx r_{o1}\parallel r_{o2}
}
\]
for an ideal ac voltage source at the input. An external load \(R_L\) at the output appears in parallel, reducing both gain and output resistance.

The input resistance seen at the source of \(M_2\) is low:
\[
\boxed{
R_{in}\approx \frac{1}{g_{m2}+g_{mb2}}
}
\]
to first order. More exactly, including finite \(r_o\) and a drain load \(R_D=r_{o1}\),
\[
R_{in}=\frac{r_{o2}+R_D}{1+(g_{m2}+g_{mb2})r_{o2}}.
\]

---

### Summary

- **Amplifier type:** common-gate NMOS stage with PMOS current-source load.
- **Input:** source of \(M_2\), \(V_{\rm in}\).
- **Output:** drain of \(M_2\), \(V_{\rm out}\).
- **Biases:** \(V_{b1}\) sets the NMOS gate; \(V_{b2}\) sets the PMOS load current.
- **Gain:** approximately  
  \[
  A_v\approx (g_{m2}+g_{mb2})(r_{o1}\parallel r_{o2})
  \]
  positive, with body effect included only when the body is not tied to the source.
- **Input resistance:** low, approximately \(1/(g_{m2}+g_{mb2})\).
- **Output resistance:** high, approximately \(r_{o1}\parallel r_{o2}\).
- **Use:** voltage/current buffer; good high-frequency behavior but limited output swing by the saturation conditions of \(M_1\) and \(M_2\).

It also provides correct DC bias and small-signal details without contradicting the topology. Meets the full-credit rule.

The circuit has **two poles** (it is second order).

Only two nodes can store independent signal energy:

1. the gate node of \(M_1\), and  
2. the output/drain node of \(M_1\) (also connected to \(M_2\)).

The gate and source/bulk of \(M_2\) are held at constant bias, so in the small-signal model they are ac ground; thus \(C_{GD2}\) and \(C_{DB2}\) simply add to the capacitance at the output node. So the circuit has **2 poles** (if the ideal model has no output conductance, one of them is at \(s=0\); with any finite output/load conductance, both are finite).

answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in Figure 19.

answer.text:
Assume the two devices are identical enhancement NMOS transistors with
\[
\beta=\mu_n C_{ox}\frac{W}{L},\qquad V_T=V_{TH},
\]
and first use the long-channel square-law model, ignoring body effect and channel-length modulation \((\lambda=0)\). Let \(V_X\) be the node between the two transistors, i.e. the drain of \(M_1\) and source of \(M_2\).

Because the gates are tied together, the lower device has a larger gate–source voltage than the upper one. With equal currents and identical devices, the pair cannot both be saturated in the ideal long-channel model. In the useful “on” region, \(M_2\) is saturated while \(M_1\) is in triode. The pair behaves like one NMOS with
\[
\left(\frac{W}{L}\right)_{\rm eff}=\frac{W}{2L},
\qquad
\beta_{\rm eff}=\frac{\beta}{2},
\]
provided body effect is negligible.

### DC transfer characteristic

Let
\[
V_{ov}=V_{in}-V_T.
\]

**1. Cutoff:**  
If \(V_{in}<V_T\),
\[
I_D\simeq0,\qquad V_{out}=V_{DD}.
\]

**2. Saturation/active region of the composite device:**  
For \(V_{in}>V_T\) and while
\[
V_{out}\ge V_{in}-V_T,
\]
\(M_2\) is saturated and \(M_1\) is in triode. Solving
\[
\beta\left(V_{ov}V_X-\frac{V_X^2}{2}\right)
=
\frac{\beta}{2}(V_{ov}-V_X)^2
\]
gives
\[
V_X=\left(1-\frac1{\sqrt2}\right)V_{ov}
   \approx0.293\,V_{ov}.
\]
The current is therefore
\[
I_D=\frac{\beta}{4}V_{ov}^2
=\frac{\beta}{4}(V_{in}-V_T)^2,
\]
so
\[
\boxed{
V_{out}=V_{DD}-\frac{\beta R_D}{4}(V_{in}-V_T)^2
}
\]
in saturation. This is the same as a single transistor whose length is doubled.

The boundary between saturation and triode is found from
\[
V_{DD}-\frac{\beta R_D}{4}V_{ov}^2=V_{ov},
\]
so
\[
V_{ov,\rm sat}
=
\frac{2}{\beta R_D}
\left(\sqrt{1+\beta R_D V_{DD}}-1\right),
\qquad
V_{in,\rm sat}=V_T+V_{ov,\rm sat}.
\]

**3. Triode/linear region of the composite device:**  
For larger \(V_{in}\), \(V_{out}<V_{in}-V_T\), and the composite transistor enters triode:
\[
\boxed{
I_D=\frac{\beta}{2}
\left[
(V_{in}-V_T)V_{out}-\frac{V_{out}^2}{2}
\right].
}
\]
Using \(V_{DD}=V_{out}+I_D R_D\), \(V_{out}\) is the smaller solution of
\[
V_{DD}-V_{out}
=
\frac{\beta R_D}{2}
\left[
(V_{in}-V_T)V_{out}-\frac{V_{out}^2}{2}
\right].
\]
Equivalently,
\[
V_{out}
=
V_{ov}+\frac{2}{\beta R_D}
-
\sqrt{
\left(V_{ov}+\frac{2}{\beta R_D}\right)^2
-\frac{4V_{DD}}{\beta R_D}
},
\]
with \(V_{ov}=V_{in}-V_T\).

Thus the transfer characteristic is inverting: as \(V_{in}\) rises, \(V_{out}\) falls quadratically in the active region and then approaches a low voltage in triode.

### Small-signal behavior in saturation

The composite transconductance is
\[
\boxed{
g_{m,\rm eff}
=
\frac{\partial I_D}{\partial V_{in}}
=
\frac{\beta}{2}(V_{in}-V_T)
}
\]
which is one half of the transconductance of a single identical transistor biased at the same overdrive.

The internal node also moves with the input:
\[
v_X=\left(1-\frac1{\sqrt2}\right)v_{in}
\approx0.293\,v_{in}.
\]
This is why the pair does not behave like a cascode: the upper gate is not at ac ground.

If channel-length modulation is included, the stack has roughly twice the output resistance of one transistor biased at the same current:
\[
r_{o,\rm eff}\approx2r_{o,M_2},
\]
so the low-frequency voltage gain is approximately
\[
\boxed{
A_v=\frac{v_{out}}{v_{in}}
\approx
-g_{m,\rm eff}\,(R_D\parallel r_{o,\rm eff})
=
-\frac{\beta}{2}(V_{in}-V_T)
\bigl(R_D\parallel r_{o,\rm eff}\bigr).
}
\]
In the ideal long-channel case with \(r_o\to\infty\),
\[
A_v\approx -\frac{\beta}{2}(V_{in}-V_T)R_D.
\]
The stage is an inverting common-source amplifier; increasing \(V_{in}\) increases the current and lowers \(V_{out}\).

### Body-effect caveat

In an integrated circuit the p-substrate is usually grounded. Then \(M_2\) has \(V_{SB}=V_X\), so its threshold is increased:
\[
V_{T2}(V_X)
=
V_{T0}+\gamma
\left(
\sqrt{2\phi_F+V_X}-\sqrt{2\phi_F}
\right).
\]
In that case the simple \(L_{\rm eff}=2L\) equivalence is only approximate. The actual current is found by solving
\[
\beta\left(V_{ov1}V_X-\frac{V_X^2}{2}\right)
=
\frac{\beta}{2}
\left[
V_{in}-V_X-V_{T2}(V_X)
\right]^2
\]
(with the upper device saturated), and \(V_{out}=V_{DD}-I_D R_D\). Body effect reduces the current relative to the body-effect-free result and increases the effective output resistance. If each source is tied to its own body/substrate, set \(V_{T2}=V_{T0}\), and the simple doubled-length model applies.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in Figure 19.

answer.text:
Assume enhancement-mode NMOS transistors, matched long-channel devices, strong inversion, and initially neglect body effect and channel-length modulation. Let  
\[
\beta=\mu_n C_{ox}\frac{W}{L}
\]
for each transistor, and define \(V_{ov}=V_{in}-V_T\).

### Equivalent device
Because the two transistors are in series and their gates are tied together, the same drain current flows through them. They act as one composite NMOS whose effective dimensions are, for equal widths,
\[
L_{\rm eff}=L_1+L_2,
\qquad
\left(\frac WL\right)_{\rm eff}
=\frac{W}{L_1+L_2}.
\]
For identical devices, \(L_{\rm eff}=2L\) and
\[
\beta_{\rm eff}=\frac{\beta}{2}.
\]
Equivalently, for nonidentical devices,
\[
\beta_{\rm eff}=\frac{\beta_1\beta_2}{\beta_1+\beta_2},
\qquad
\frac{1}{\beta_{\rm eff}}=\frac1{\beta_1}+\frac1{\beta_2}.
\]

### Operating regions
Let \(V_X\) be the internal node (drain of \(M_1\), source of \(M_2\)).

1. **Cutoff:**  
   If \(V_{in}<V_T\), both devices are off,
   \[
   I_D\approx0,\qquad V_{out}\approx V_{DD}.
   \]

2. **Normal high-output/saturation region of the composite:**  
   Here \(M_2\) is saturated and \(M_1\) is in the triode region. Equating their currents gives
   \[
   V_X=\left(1-\frac{1}{\sqrt2}\right)(V_{in}-V_T)
   \approx0.293\,(V_{in}-V_T),
   \]
   and
   \[
   I_D=\frac{\beta}{4}(V_{in}-V_T)^2.
   \]
   With the resistive load,
   \[
   \boxed{V_{out}=V_{DD}-\frac{\beta R_D}{4}(V_{in}-V_T)^2}
   \]
   as long as
   \[
   V_{in}>V_T
   \quad\text{and}\quad
   V_{out}\ge V_{in}-V_T.
   \]
   The equality \(V_{out}=V_{in}-V_T\) is the edge between saturation and triode.

3. **Low-output/triode region of the composite:**  
   If \(V_{out}<V_{in}-V_T\), \(M_2\) also enters triode; both devices are then in triode and the stack is equivalent to one long-channel transistor:
   \[
   I_D=\frac{\beta}{2}
   \left[(V_{in}-V_T)V_{out}-\frac{V_{out}^2}{2}\right].
   \]
   The actual \(V_{out}\) is found together with
   \[
   V_{out}=V_{DD}-I_D R_D.
   \]
   At the boundary, both expressions give
   \(I_D=\beta(V_{in}-V_T)^2/4\).

### Small-signal behavior
Biased in the composite saturation region, the stage is a resistor-loaded common-source amplifier using the equivalent long-channel NMOS. Its small-signal transconductance is
\[
\boxed{g_{m,\rm eff}
=\frac{\beta}{2}(V_{in}-V_T)
=\sqrt{\beta I_D}}
\]
for matched devices. Ignoring channel-length modulation,
\[
\boxed{A_v=\frac{v_{out}}{v_{in}}
\approx -g_{m,\rm eff}R_D
=-\frac{\beta R_D}{2}(V_{in}-V_T).}
\]
With finite output resistance,
\[
A_v\approx -g_{m,\rm eff}(R_D\parallel r_{o,\rm eff}).
\]
The series connection raises the output resistance compared with one transistor; to first order it behaves like a transistor with doubled channel length, so its channel-length-modulation parameter is roughly halved and \(r_o\) is correspondingly increased.

### Body-effect note
If both NMOS bodies are tied to the common substrate/ground, \(M_2\) experiences body effect because its source is at \(V_X>0\). Then replace the threshold of \(M_2\) by
\[
V_{T2}=V_{T0}+\gamma\left(
\sqrt{2\phi_F+V_X}-\sqrt{2\phi_F}
\right),
\]
and solve
\[
\beta_1\!\left[(V_{in}-V_{T1})V_X-\frac{V_X^2}{2}\right]
=
\frac{\beta_2}{2}
\left[V_{in}-V_X-V_{T2}(V_X)\right]^2
\]
for \(V_X\). This lowers the current and gain. If each body is connected to its own source, the simple \(L_{\rm eff}=L_1+L_2\) result is exact in the long-channel square-law model.

In summary, the circuit is a resistor-loaded common-source NMOS in which the series pair behaves as a single NMOS of approximately doubled channel length: it has half the current drive for the same gate overdrive, higher output resistance, and reduced short-channel effects.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in Figure 19.

answer.text:
Assume the two enhancement NMOS devices are identical, with the usual long-channel square-law model,
\[
\beta=\mu_n C_{ox}\frac{W}{L},\qquad 
I_D=\frac{\beta}{2}(V_{GS}-V_T)^2(1+\lambda V_{DS})
\]

In the saturated part of its characteristic it is not true that both transistors are saturated: the upper device \(M_2\) is in saturation and the lower device \(M_1\) is in its triode/linear region. The pair behaves as one NMOS with approximately
\[
L_{\rm eff}=L_1+L_2=2L,\qquad
\beta_{\rm eff}=\frac{\beta}{2},
\]
assuming equal devices.

Thus, with \(V_{ov}=V_{in}-V_T>0\) and \(V_{DS}=V_{out}\) measured from the top drain to ground,
\[
I_D=
\begin{cases}
0, & V_{ov}\le 0,\\[4pt]
\dfrac{\beta}{2}\left(V_{ov}V_{out}
-\dfrac{1}{2}V_{out}^{\,2}\right),
& 0<V_{out}<V_{ov},\\[10pt]
\dfrac{\beta}{4}V_{ov}^{\,2},
& V_{out}\ge V_{ov}.
\end{cases}
\]
The first non-zero region is the composite triode region; the last is the composite saturation region.

At \(V_{in}\le V_T\), the stack is off:
\[
I_D\approx0,\qquad V_{out}=V_{DD}.
\]

For \(V_{in}>V_T\), while the stack is saturated,
\[
V_{out}=V_{DD}-\frac{\beta R_D}{4}(V_{in}-V_T)^2,
\]
valid as long as
\[
V_{out}\ge V_{in}-V_T.
\]
Hence the circuit is an inverting amplifier: increasing \(V_{in}\) increases the current and lowers \(V_{out}\).

The boundary between saturation and triode occurs when
\[
V_{out}=V_{in}-V_T.
\]
Equivalently, the overdrive at the boundary is
\[
V_{ov,B}
=
\frac{2}{\beta R_D}
\left(\sqrt{1+\beta R_DV_{DD}}-1\right),
\]
and
\[
V_{in,B}=V_T+V_{ov,B}.
\]

For \(V_{in}>V_{in,B}\), the stack enters triode. Then \(V_{out}\) satisfies
\[
V_{DD}
=
V_{out}
+
R_D\frac{\beta}{2}
\left[
(V_{in}-V_T)V_{out}
-\frac{1}{2}V_{out}^{\,2}
\right],
\]
or, equivalently,
\[
V_{in}
=
V_T+\frac{V_{out}}{2}
+
\frac{2(V_{DD}-V_{out})}
{\beta R_DV_{out}}.
\]
As \(V_{in}\) is increased further, \(V_{out}\to0\) in the ideal long-channel model.

The internal node voltage \(V_X=V_{D1}=V_{S2}\) in the saturated region is
\[
V_X=\left(1-\frac{1}{\sqrt2}\right)(V_{in}-V_T)
\approx0.293\,(V_{in}-V_T).
\]
In the triode region both devices are in triode; in the deep triode limit \(V_X\approx V_{out}/2\).

## 3. Small-signal model

At a bias point in the saturated region, let \(V_{IN}\) be the dc gate voltage. The equivalent common-source transistor has
\[
g_{m,\rm eq}
=
\frac{\partial I_D}{\partial V_{in}}
=
\frac{\beta}{2}(V_{IN}-V_T)
=
\sqrt{\beta I_D}.
\]
Its intrinsic output resistance is increased by the series connection. If each device has channel-length modulation parameter \(\lambda\) and \(\lambda L\approx\) constant,
\[
\lambda_{\rm eff}\approx\frac{\lambda}{2},
\qquad
r_{o,\rm eq}\approx\frac{2}{\lambda I_D}
\]
at the same operating current \(I_D\). More accurately, with \(M_1\) in triode and \(M_2\) in saturation,
\[
R_{o,\rm stack}
\approx
\frac{g_{ds1}+g_{m2}+g_{ds2}}{g_{ds1}g_{ds2}}
\approx \frac{2}{g_{ds2}},
\]
since for equal devices \(g_{ds1}\approx g_{m2}\). If channel-length modulation is neglected, \(r_{o,\rm eq}\to\infty\).

The loaded voltage gain is therefore
\[
A_v=\frac{v_{out}}{v_{in}}
=
-g_{m,\rm eq}\bigl(R_D\parallel r_{o,\rm eq}\bigr),
\]
with the minus sign indicating phase inversion. If \(r_{o,\rm eq}\gg R_D\),
\[
A_v\approx
-\frac{\beta R_D}{2}(V_{IN}-V_T).
\]

## Summary

- Low \(V_{in}<V_T\): both NMOS off; \(V_{out}=V_{DD}\).
- Moderate \(V_{in}\): \(M_2\) saturated, \(M_1\) triode; the pair behaves as one NMOS with twice the channel length:
  \[
  I_D\approx\frac{\beta}{4}(V_{in}-V_T)^2,
  \qquad
  V_{out}=V_{DD}-R_D I_D.
  \]
- High \(V_{in}\): the equivalent device enters triode and \(V_{out}\) approaches ground.
- The series connection reduces current/transconductance for a given \(V_{ov}\) and increases output resistance; hence it emulates a longer-channel NMOS. If the bodies are not tied to their sources, the body effect raises the threshold of the upper device and modifies these expressions, but the qualitative behavior is unchanged.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit of Figure 20.

answer.text:
Assume the two devices are enhancement NMOS transistors operating in saturation, and neglect body effect and parasitic capacitances for a low-frequency analysis. The current source \(I_1\) is ideal, so in the small-signal model it is an open circuit. \(M_1\) is a source follower that drives the source of the common-gate stage \(M_2\).

Let
\[
v_x=\text{small-signal voltage at the common source node},\quad
v_o=v_{\text{out}},\quad v_i=v_{\text{in}}.
\]
With \(V_b\) treated as a dc bias, the small-signal KCL equations are
\[
g_{m1}(v_i-v_x)-\frac{v_x}{r_{o1}}
-g_{m2}v_x+\frac{v_o-v_x}{r_{o2}}=0,
\]
\[
-g_{m2}v_x+\frac{v_o-v_x}{r_{o2}}+\frac{v_o}{R_D}=0.
\]

### Voltage gain
Solving gives, including finite transistor output resistances,
\[
\boxed{
A_v=\frac{v_o}{v_i}
=
\frac{g_{m1}R_D(1+g_{m2}r_{o2})}
{(R_D+r_{o2})(g_{m1}+1/r_{o1})+(1+g_{m2}r_{o2})}
}
\]
The gain is **positive**, i.e. the stage is non-inverting from \(V_{\rm in}\) to \(V_{\rm out}\): increasing \(V_{\rm in}\) turns \(M_1\) on harder, reduces \(M_2\)'s current, and therefore raises \(V_{\rm out}\).

For the usual approximation \(g_m r_o\gg 1\) and \(R_D\ll r_o\),
\[
\boxed{
A_v\approx
\frac{g_{m1}g_{m2}}{g_{m1}+g_{m2}}R_D
}
\]
or, if \(g_{m1}=g_{m2}=g_m\),
\[
\boxed{A_v\approx \frac{g_mR_D}{2}.}
\]
Equivalently, the source-follower first drives the low input impedance \(R_{\rm in,CG}\approx 1/g_{m2}\) of the common-gate stage:
\[
v_x\approx \frac{g_{m1}}{g_{m1}+g_{m2}}v_i,
\qquad
v_o\approx g_{m2}R_D\,v_x.
\]
If an incremental signal \(v_b\) is also applied at \(V_b\), the ideal result becomes
\[
v_o\approx
\frac{g_{m1}g_{m2}}{g_{m1}+g_{m2}}R_D\,(v_i-v_b),
\]
so the circuit responds mainly to the differential voltage \(v_i-v_b\); the ideal tail current suppresses common-mode changes.

### DC bias and saturation
Let \(V_X\) be the dc voltage at the common source node and \(I_{D1},I_{D2}\) the drain currents. Then
\[
I_{D1}+I_{D2}=I_1,
\qquad
V_{\rm out}=V_{DD}-I_{D2}R_D.
\]
Equivalently, the tail current is steered between the two transistors by \(V_{\rm in}-V_b\).  
Saturation requires approximately
\[
V_{\rm in}-V_X>V_{Tn},\qquad
V_b-V_X>V_{Tn},
\]
\[
V_{DD}\gtrsim V_{\rm in}-V_{Tn},
\qquad
V_{\rm out}\ge V_b-V_{Tn},
\]
plus enough voltage at the common source node to keep the current sink \(I_1\) in its valid operating region. The hard output range is approximately
\[
V_{DD}-I_1R_D \lesssim V_{\rm out}\le V_{DD},
\]
but saturation of \(M_2\) further restricts the lower end.

### Resistances
The input resistance at the gate of \(M_1\) is ideally infinite at low frequency. The small-signal output resistance at \(V_{\rm out}\), including \(R_D\), is
\[
\boxed{
R_{\rm out}
=
R_D\parallel
\left[
r_{o2}+(1+g_{m2}r_{o2})
\frac{r_{o1}}{1+g_{m1}r_{o1}}
\right].
}
\]
If \(R_D\) is considered an external load, omit the parallel \(R_D\) term. In the common approximation \(g_m r_o\gg1\),
\[
R_{\rm out}\approx R_D
\parallel
\left[
r_{o2}\left(1+\frac{g_{m2}}{g_{m1}}\right)+\frac1{g_{m1}}
\right],
\]
and if \(R_D\) is much smaller than the active output resistance, then simply
\[
R_{\rm out}\approx R_D.
\]

Thus the circuit is a non-inverting single-ended amplifier/level-shifting gain stage: a source follower drives a common-gate stage, with voltage gain roughly the loaded transconductance
\[
G_m\approx \frac{g_{m1}g_{m2}}{g_{m1}+g_{m2}}
\]
times \(R_D\). Its output bandwidth would be set mainly by \(R_{\rm out}\) and the total capacitance at the output node, while the common-source node is a low-impedance node because it is driven by both transistor source transconductances.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit of Figure 20.

answer.text:
The circuit in Figure 20 is a **source follower driving a common-gate stage**:

- \(M_1\) is an NMOS common-drain (source-follower) device; its drain is at ac ground through \(V_{DD}\).
- \(M_2\) is an NMOS common-gate device; its gate is biased at \(V_b\) and is an ac ground.
- The sources of \(M_1\) and \(M_2\) are tied together and biased by the tail current source \(I_1\).
- The output is taken at the drain of \(M_2\), with \(R_D\) as the load resistor.
- The circuit is essentially one half of a differential pair, used as a single-ended, high-input-impedance, non-inverting voltage amplifier.

### DC bias
Neglecting channel-length modulation and body effect,  
\[
I_{D1}+I_{D2}=I_1,\qquad
V_{\rm out}=V_{DD}-I_{D2}R_D .
\]
The common-source voltage \(V_S\) is set by the two gate-source voltages:
\[
I_{D1}=\tfrac12 k_1(V_{\rm in}-V_S-V_{T1})^2,\qquad
I_{D2}=\tfrac12 k_2(V_b-V_S-V_{T2})^2 .
\]
If the devices are matched and quiescent \(V_{\rm in}=V_b\), then
\[
I_{D1}=I_{D2}=\frac{I_1}{2},\qquad
V_{\rm out}=V_{DD}-\frac{I_1}{2}R_D .
\]
Both devices must remain in saturation:
\[
V_{DD}-V_S>V_{GS1}-V_T,\qquad
V_{\rm out}-V_S>V_{GS2}-V_T .
\]

### Small-signal gain
Let \(v_i\) be a small-signal variation of \(V_{\rm in}\), and set the bias \(v_b=0\) for an ideal bias supply. Ignoring \(r_o\) and body effect,
\[
v_s=\frac{g_{m1}}{g_{m1}+g_{m2}}\,v_i,
\]
where \(v_s\) is the small-signal voltage of the common-source node. For the common-gate stage,
\[
v_{\rm out}=g_{m2}R_D\,v_s .
\]
Hence
\[
\boxed{
A_v\equiv \frac{v_{\rm out}}{v_i}
=
\frac{g_{m1}g_{m2}}{g_{m1}+g_{m2}}\,R_D
}
\]
with the output **in phase** with \(v_i\).

If the two transistors are matched and equally biased, \(g_{m1}=g_{m2}=g_m\), so
\[
\boxed{A_v=\frac{1}{2}g_m R_D}
\]
and the effective transconductance is
\[
G_m=\frac{g_{m1}g_{m2}}{g_{m1}+g_{m2}}
\quad\xrightarrow{\text{matched}}\quad
\frac{g_m}{2}.
\]

If \(V_b\) is not an ac ground but has a small-signal component \(v_b\), the ideal-tail-current result becomes
\[
\boxed{
v_{\rm out}
=
\frac{g_{m1}g_{m2}}{g_{m1}+g_{m2}}R_D\,(v_i-v_b)
}
\]
(no body effect). Thus the stage amplifies the difference between the two gate voltages; a positive change in \(v_b\) decreases the output.

### Input and output resistance
At low frequencies the input is the gate of \(M_1\):
\[
\boxed{R_{\rm in}\approx\infty}
\]
(neglecting gate leakage and capacitances).

To first order, ignoring \(r_{o1},r_{o2}\) and body effect,
\[
\boxed{R_{\rm out}\approx R_D}.
\]
Including the finite output resistance of \(M_2\) but neglecting the other nonidealities gives approximately
\[
R_{\rm out}\approx
R_D\parallel
r_{o2}\left(1+\frac{g_{m2}}{g_{m1}}\right).
\]
For a more exact low-frequency model, define
\[
G_1=g_{m1}+g_{mb1}+g_{ds1},\qquad
G_2=g_{m2}+g_{mb2}+g_{ds2},
\]
with \(g_{ds}=1/r_o\), \(g_{mb}=0\) if the body is tied to the source, and \(g_t=1/R_{\rm tail}\) (\(g_t=0\) for an ideal current source). Then the small-signal output is
\[
v_{\rm out}
=
\frac{
R_D\!\left[
G_2g_{m1}v_i
-
g_{m2}(G_1+g_t)v_b
\right]
}{
G_1+G_2+g_t+g_{ds2}(G_1+g_t)R_D
},
\]
and
\[
R_{\rm out}
=
R_D\parallel
\frac{G_1+G_2+g_t}{g_{ds2}(G_1+g_t)}.
\]

### Frequency-response note
At high frequency, the common-source node is a low-impedance node, about
\[
R_s\sim \frac{1}{g_{m1}+g_{m2}},
\]
so it forms a high-frequency pole with the source capacitances. The output node forms the dominant pole with
\[
R_{\rm out}\parallel R_L
\]
and the total output capacitance. The source-follower input has high impedance and avoids strong Miller multiplication of the input capacitance, which is a principal reason for using this source-follower/common-gate combination.

Overall, the circuit is a non-inverting voltage amplifier whose gain is set by \(R_D\) and the effective transconductance of the series source-follower/common-gate combination; for matched devices its low-frequency gain is approximately \(g_mR_D/2\).

answers.question: Analyze the circuit of Figure 20.

answer.text:
Figure 20 is a single-ended **current-steered amplifier**.  \(M_1\) operates as a **source follower** (common drain) and \(M_2\) as a **common-gate** stage.  The current source \(I_1\) is the tail bias; the signal current is steered between \(M_1\) and \(M_2\).  It is not a normal cascode because the two transistors do not carry the same signal current; their drain currents sum to \(I_1\).

Let \(V_S\) be the voltage of the common source node and let \(V_b\) be an ac ground/bias voltage for small-signal analysis.

## dc bias
\[
I_{D1}+I_{D2}=I_1,\qquad
V_{\rm out}=V_{DD}-I_{D2}R_D .
\]
If \(M_1,M_2\) are matched and \(V_{in,dc}=V_b\), then
\[
I_{D1}=I_{D2}=\frac{I_1}{2},\qquad
V_{\rm out}=V_{DD}-\frac{I_1R_D}{2}.
\]
For each device, the transconductance is then approximately
\[
g_m=\sqrt{\mu_n C_{ox}\frac{W}{L}I_1}
\]
when both devices are identical and carry \(I_1/2\).

For saturation:
\[
V_b-V_S>V_{T2},\qquad V_{in}-V_S>V_{T1},
\]
\[
V_{\rm out}\ge V_b-V_{T2}
\]
for \(M_2\), and the tail current sink must have enough voltage at its terminal, i.e. \(V_S>V_{\rm CS,sat}\).

## small-signal voltage gain
First neglect \(r_o\), body effect, and finite tail-source impedance.  Let
\[
i_{d1}=g_{m1}(v_{in}-v_S),\qquad
i_{d2}=g_{m2}(0-v_S)=-g_{m2}v_S.
\]
Since the ideal tail current is constant,
\[
i_{d1}+i_{d2}=0
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
v_S=\frac{g_{m1}}{g_{m1}+g_{m2}}v_{in}.
\]
The output voltage is
\[
v_{\rm out}=-i_{d2}R_D
      =\frac{g_{m1}g_{m2}}{g_{m1}+g_{m2}}R_D\,v_{in}.
\]
Hence
\[
\boxed{
A_v=\frac{v_{\rm out}}{v_{in}}
\approx
\frac{g_{m1}g_{m2}}{g_{m1}+g_{m2}}R_D
}
\]
and the stage is **non-inverting**.

Including body effect, but still neglecting \(r_o\),
\[
\boxed{
A_v\approx
\frac{g_{m1}(g_{m2}+g_{mb2})R_D}
{g_{m1}+g_{mb1}+g_{m2}+g_{mb2}}.
}
\]
If the devices are identical, body effect cancels in the matched result:
\[
\boxed{A_v\approx \frac{g_mR_D}{2}}.
\]
If \(M_1\) is made much stronger than \(M_2\), \(g_{m1}\gg g_{m2}\), then
\[
A_v\approx g_{m2}R_D,
\]
i.e. the source follower nearly drives the common-gate stage with unity source-follower gain.

If both gates are driven differentially and the devices are matched,
\[
\boxed{
v_{\rm out}\approx\frac{g_mR_D}{2}\,(v_{in}-v_b)
}
\]
for small signals.  Thus \(V_b\) must be a clean dc/ac-ground if only \(V_{in}\) is the input; otherwise it acts as the other differential input.

## exact low-frequency small-signal result
Define, including body effect and channel-length modulation,
\[
G_1=g_{m1}+g_{mb1}+\frac{1}{r_{o1}},\qquad
G_2=g_{m2}+g_{mb2}+\frac{1}{r_{o2}},
\]
\[
G_s=G_1+G_2+\frac{1}{R_T},
\]
where \(R_T\) is the small-signal output resistance of \(I_1\) (\(R_T\to\infty\) for an ideal current sink).  Then
\[
\boxed{
A_v=
\frac{g_{m1}G_2R_D\,r_{o2}}
{G_s r_{o2}+\left(G_1+\frac{1}{R_T}\right)R_D}
}
\]
with the sign positive.  Set \(g_{mb1}=g_{mb2}=0\) to ignore body effect and let \(r_{o1},r_{o2}\to\infty\) to recover the simple result above.

## input and output resistances
At low frequency the input gate draws no current:
\[
\boxed{R_{in}\approx\infty.}
\]

The low input resistance of the common-gate stage seen by \(M_1\) is approximately
\[
R_{in,M2}\approx\frac{1}{g_{m2}+g_{mb2}},
\]
or more exactly
\[
R_{in,M2}=
\frac{R_D+r_{o2}}
{1+(g_{m2}+g_{mb2})r_{o2}}.
\]

For output resistance, first define the small-signal resistance from the common source node to ground through \(M_1\) and the tail source:
\[
R_X=
\left(
g_{m1}+g_{mb1}+\frac{1}{r_{o1}}+\frac{1}{R_T}
\right)^{-1}.
\]
Then the resistance looking into the drain of \(M_2\), before \(R_D\), is
\[
\boxed{
R_{o,M2}
=
r_{o2}+\left[1+(g_{m2}+g_{mb2})r_{o2}\right]R_X.
}
\]
Including \(R_D\),
\[
\boxed{
R_{\rm out}=R_D\parallel R_{o,M2}.
}
\]
For ideal transistors with \(r_{o2}\to\infty\), \(R_{o,M2}\to\infty\), so the output resistance is simply \(R_D\) when \(R_D\) is included.

## qualitative behavior
- Input increase \(\Rightarrow V_S\) increases \(\Rightarrow V_{GS2}\) decreases \(\Rightarrow I_{D2}\) decreases \(\Rightarrow V_{\rm out}\) increases. Hence the amplifier is non-inverting.
- The circuit has very high input resistance and low feedback from output to input; there is no direct \(C_{gd}\) path from \(V_{in}\) to \(V_{\rm out}\).  Thus it is less subject to Miller multiplication than an ordinary common-source stage.
- For equal devices its effective transconductance is \(g_m/2\), not \(g_m\).  To obtain nearly full \(g_{m2}R_D\) gain, \(M_1\) must have \(g_{m1}\gg g_{m2}\) so that the source follower can drive the low input resistance of the common-gate stage.
- \(V_b\) sets the current split and the operating point; with matched devices and a balanced dc input, choose \(V_{in,dc}=V_b\) so that \(I_{D1}=I_{D2}=I_1/2\).
- Output swing is limited by \(M_2\) leaving saturation, approximately when \(V_{\rm out}<V_b-V_{T2}\), and by the tail current-source headroom. If \(V_{in}\) drives far enough, one of \(M_1,M_2\) turns off and the output clips near \(V_{DD}\) or near \(V_{DD}-I_1R_D\).

answers.question: Explain why the output impedance of the circuit shown in Figure 21 can be inductive.

answer.text:
The upper device \(M_1\) operates as a source follower, with \(M_2\) acting as a current-sink load. For small-signal output impedance, \(V_{\rm in}\) is set to zero, so the gate of \(M_1\) is connected to ac ground through \(R_S\). The important feedback element is \(C_{gs1}\): the output node (source of \(M_1\)) is capacitively coupled back to its gate.

Let \(C=C_{gs1}\), \(g_m=g_{m1}\), and let \(g_o=1/r_{o1}+1/r_{o2}\) (plus \(g_{mb1}\) if body effect is included). KCL at the gate gives  
\[
v_g=v_o\frac{j\omega R_S C}{1+j\omega R_S C}.
\]
Thus the small-signal current drawn at the output is approximately
\[
Y_o=\frac{i_o}{v_o}
\approx g_o+\frac{g_m+j\omega C}{1+j\omega R_S C},
\]
so
\[
Z_o=\frac{v_o}{i_o}
\approx
\frac{1+j\omega R_S C}
{g_m+g_o+j\omega C\left(1+R_S g_o\right)}.
\]

For the usual case where \(g_o\) is small, its imaginary part is
\[
\operatorname{Im}(Z_o)
\approx
\frac{\omega C\,(R_S g_{m1}-1)}
{g_{m1}^{\,2}+\omega^2 C^2}.
\]
Therefore,
\[
\boxed{
R_S g_{m1}>1
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\operatorname{Im}(Z_o)>0
}
\]
so the output impedance has an inductive component, because an inductor has \(Z=j\omega L\) (positive imaginary part).

Physically, the \(R_S-C_{gs1}\) network introduces a phase shift in the gate-source voltage when the output is perturbed. The resulting small-signal transistor current \(g_m v_{gs}\) acquires a component that lags the applied output voltage. A lagging current is exactly what an inductor produces. If \(R_S\) is too small, or \(g_{m1}\) too small, then \(R_Sg_{m1}<1\) and the output impedance remains capacitive rather than inductive.

In a real circuit, the finite output resistance of \(M_2\) and other parasitic capacitances appear in parallel with this active inductance. They lower the \(Q\), limit the frequency range, and eventually make the impedance capacitive again at high frequency, but the source-follower feedback can indeed make \(Z_{\rm out}\) look inductive over a useful band.

It also captures the low/high-frequency limiting behavior and physical mechanism, with only minor extra modeling details that do not affect the conclusion.

answers.question: Explain why the output impedance of the circuit shown in Figure 21 can be inductive.

answer.text:
The output can be inductive because the source follower \(M_1\) with a finite gate resistance \(R_S\) behaves like an active gyrator: its gate–source capacitance is converted by the transistor transconductance into an equivalent inductance.

For small-signal output impedance, set \(V_{\rm in}=0\). The gate of \(M_1\) is then ac-connected to ground only through \(R_S\). If the output (source of \(M_1\)) is disturbed by a small voltage \(v_o\), the gate voltage follows a delayed fraction of \(v_o\) through \(C_{gs}\):

\[
v_g \approx \frac{sR_S C_{gs}}{1+sR_S C_{gs}}\,v_o .
\]

Therefore the small-signal current supplied by \(M_1\) into the output is approximately

\[
i_o \approx g_m(v_o-v_g)
     = \frac{g_m}{1+sR_S C_{gs}}\,v_o .
\]

Thus the output admittance contributed by \(M_1\) is

\[
Y_{\rm out}\approx \frac{g_m}{1+sR_S C_{gs}},
\]

so

\[
Z_{\rm out}=\frac1{Y_{\rm out}}
\approx \frac{1+sR_S C_{gs}}{g_m}
= \frac{1}{g_m}+s\frac{R_S C_{gs}}{g_m}.
\]

With \(s=j\omega\),

\[
Z_{\rm out}\approx \frac{1}{g_m}
+ j\omega\left(\frac{R_S C_{gs}}{g_m}\right)
= R_{\rm eq}+j\omega L_{\rm eq},
\qquad
L_{\rm eq}=\frac{R_S C_{gs}}{g_m}>0.
\]

A positive imaginary part means an inductive reactance. Physically, the output voltage is fed back to the gate through \(C_{gs}\), but the gate does not follow immediately because of \(R_S\); the resulting phase lag in the controlled transistor current makes the output look inductive.

More exactly, the load transistor \(M_2\), the output resistances \(r_{o1},r_{o2}\), body effect, and parasitic output capacitance appear in parallel/series with this inductive term. Hence the output impedance is not a pure inductance: it is inductive only over a frequency band. At very low frequencies it is mainly resistive, and at very high frequencies the output capacitance dominates so it becomes capacitive again. If \(R_S\) is too large, this inductive behavior can cause peaking or ringing when the stage drives a capacitive load.

answers.question: Explain why the output impedance of the circuit shown in Figure 21 can be inductive.

answer.text:
The circuit is basically a source follower \(M_1\) with a current-source load \(M_2\). Its output can look inductive because the source follower’s gate is not an ideal ac ground: it is returned to ground through the finite source resistance \(R_S\), and the gate–source capacitance \(C_{gs}\) couples the output node back to the gate.

For output impedance, set \(V_{\rm in}=0\), apply a test voltage \(v_o\) at \(V_{\rm out}\), and measure the current. The gate voltage is then approximately

\[
v_g=\frac{j\omega R_S C_{gs}}{1+j\omega R_S C_{gs}}\,v_o .
\]

At very low frequency, \(v_g\approx 0\), so the gate is effectively grounded and the output resistance is approximately

\[
R_o \simeq \frac{1}{g_{m1}+g_{mb1}}\parallel r_{o1}\parallel r_{o2},
\]

which is real. As frequency rises, \(C_{gs}\) makes the gate voltage follow the output with a phase shift. Hence \(v_{gs}=v_g-v_o\) is no longer in phase with the applied output voltage, and the current drawn by the transistor has a quadrature component. A current that lags the applied voltage is exactly the behavior of an inductive reactance.

A small-signal calculation (neglecting \(r_o\) and load capacitance for simplicity, and writing \(G=1/R_S\)) gives

\[
Y_{\rm out}
=
\frac{G(g_{m1}+sC_{gs})}{G+sC_{gs}}+Y_L ,
\]

so the source-follower part is

\[
Z_{\rm out,M1}(s)
\simeq
\frac{1+sR_S C_{gs}}{g_{m1}+sC_{gs}}
=
\frac{1}{g_{m1}}\,
\frac{1+sR_S C_{gs}}{1+sC_{gs}/g_{m1}} .
\]

At low-to-moderate frequencies,

\[
Z_{\rm out}
\simeq
\frac{1}{g_{m1}}
+
j\omega
\frac{C_{gs}}{g_{m1}}
\left(R_S-\frac{1}{g_{m1}}\right)
=
\frac{1}{g_{m1}}+j\omega L_{\rm eq}.
\]

Thus the output appears as a resistance in series with an equivalent inductance

\[
L_{\rm eq}\approx \frac{R_S C_{gs}}{g_{m1}}
\qquad (g_{m1}R_S\gg 1).
\]

This inductive behavior occurs only when the phase shift is in the correct direction, roughly \(g_{m1}R_S>1\), and over a limited frequency range. If \(R_S=0\) or is too small, the gate is essentially grounded and the output impedance is not inductive. The output/load capacitance can resonate with this equivalent inductance, causing peaking; the finite output resistances of \(M_1\) and \(M_2\) damp that resonance.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in Figure 22.

answer.text:
### Circuit identification
Assuming the MOS symbols are enhancement NMOS transistors with sources/body tied to ground:

- \(M_1\) is an NMOS common-source stage. Its gate is node \(X\), its drain is \(V_{\rm out}\), and \(R_{D1}\) is the drain load from \(V_{DD}\).
- \(M_2\) is a feedback NMOS: drain at \(X\), source grounded, gate at \(V_{\rm out}\).
- The input is a current \(I_{\rm in}\) injected into node \(X\) (arrow upward). If the current arrow is reversed, reverse the signs below.

Thus the circuit is a **current-input, voltage-output positive-feedback stage**. \(M_1\) inverts from \(X\) to \(V_{\rm out}\), and \(M_2\) effectively inverts again from \(V_{\rm out}\) back to node \(X\).

### Feedback polarity
\[
X\uparrow \;\Rightarrow\; V_{\rm out}\downarrow
\]
A lower \(V_{\rm out}\) reduces \(M_2\)'s gate voltage, so \(M_2\) sinks less current from \(X\). With \(I_{\rm in}\) still injecting current into \(X\), \(X\) rises further. Hence the loop is regenerative:
\[
\boxed{\text{positive feedback}}
\]
For small-signal operation this gives an increased (or negative) input resistance. For large-signal operation it can produce hysteresis, latching, or oscillation.

---

## D.C. / large-signal operation

Let
\[
K_i=\mu_n C_{ox}\left(\frac{W}{L}\right)_i,\qquad V_T=V_{Tn},
\]
and neglect gate leakage. The two D.C. balance equations are
\[
I_{\rm in}=I_{D2}(V_X,V_{\rm out}),
\]
\[
I_{D1}(V_X,V_{\rm out})=\frac{V_{DD}-V_{\rm out}}{R_{D1}}.
\]

In the usual active/saturation region,
\[
I_{D1}=\frac{K_1}{2}(V_X-V_T)^2,
\qquad
I_{D2}=\frac{K_2}{2}(V_{\rm out}-V_T)^2.
\]
Then
\[
V_{\rm out}=V_T+\sqrt{\frac{2I_{\rm in}}{K_2}},
\]
\[
V_X=V_T+
\sqrt{\frac{2}{K_1R_{D1}}
\left(V_{DD}-V_{\rm out}\right)} .
\]
These are valid while
\[
V_{\rm out}\ge V_X-V_T\qquad (M_1\ \text{saturated}),
\]
\[
V_X\ge V_{\rm out}-V_T\qquad (M_2\ \text{saturated}).
\]
In this region, increasing \(I_{\rm in}\) increases \(V_{\rm out}\), which requires a lower \(V_X\):
\[
\frac{dV_X}{dI_{\rm in}}<0
\]
so the input exhibits **negative differential resistance**.

If \(M_2\) enters the triode region,
\[
I_{D2}=K_2\left[(V_{\rm out}-V_T)V_X-\frac{V_X^2}{2}\right],
\]
and if \(M_1\) enters triode,
\[
I_{D1}=K_1\left[(V_X-V_T)V_{\rm out}-\frac{V_{\rm out}^2}{2}\right].
\]
Those regions determine the actual clamped high/low states and switching levels.

### Qualitative states
- **High-output state:** For small positive \(I_{\rm in}\), \(M_1\) may be off/weak, \(V_{\rm out}\approx V_{DD}\), and \(M_2\) operates in triode, sinking the input current. This is the stable “untriggered” state.
- As \(I_{\rm in}\) increases, \(X\) rises; \(M_1\) turns on, pulling \(V_{\rm out}\) down. This reduces \(M_2\)'s current, allowing \(X\) to rise further: regeneration occurs.
- **Low-output/latched state:** \(V_X\) becomes high, \(M_1\) holds \(V_{\rm out}\) low, and \(M_2\) is cut off or very weak because its gate is low. The state can be held by charge stored on the gate capacitance. A reset is needed to discharge \(X\) and return the circuit to the high-output state.
- Approximate switching current: when \(V_X\) reaches the trip point \(V_{\rm trip}\) of the \(M_1\)-\(R_{D1}\) inverter,
\[
I_{\rm th}\approx I_{D2}\big(V_X=V_{\rm trip},\,V_{\rm out}\approx V_{DD}\big).
\]
If \(M_2\) is in triode at that instant,
\[
I_{\rm th}\approx
K_2\left[(V_{DD}-V_T)V_{\rm trip}
-\frac{V_{\rm trip}^2}{2}\right],
\]
provided \(V_{\rm trip}<V_{DD}-V_T\); otherwise use the saturation expression. The reverse level is much lower because \(M_2\) is off/weak when \(V_{\rm out}\) is low. This difference gives hysteresis.

---

## Small-signal analysis

At a bias point in which both devices are active, define
\[
g_{m1}=K_1(V_X-V_T),\quad g_{m2}=K_2(V_{\rm out}-V_T),
\]
\[
r_{o1}=\frac{1}{g_{o1}},\quad r_{o2}=\frac{1}{g_{o2}},
\qquad
R_L=R_{D1}\parallel r_{o1}.
\]
Small-signal KCL gives
\[
i_{\rm in}=g_{m2}v_{\rm out}+g_{o2}v_X,
\]
\[
g_{m1}v_X+g_{o1}v_{\rm out}+\frac{v_{\rm out}}{R_{D1}}=0,
\]
so
\[
v_{\rm out}=-g_{m1}R_L\,v_X.
\]
Therefore
\[
i_{\rm in}
=
\left[g_{o2}-g_{m1}g_{m2}R_L\right]v_X.
\]

Define the positive-feedback loop gain
\[
\boxed{T=g_{m1}g_{m2}R_L\,r_{o2}
      =\frac{g_{m1}g_{m2}R_L}{g_{o2}} }.
\]
Then
\[
\boxed{R_{\rm in}
=\frac{v_X}{i_{\rm in}}
=\frac{r_{o2}}{1-T}}
\]
and
\[
\boxed{\frac{v_{\rm out}}{i_{\rm in}}
=
-\frac{g_{m1}R_Lr_{o2}}{1-T}}.
\]
With the input current source open-circuited for output-resistance calculation,
\[
\boxed{R_{\rm out}
=\frac{R_L}{1-T}}.
\]

Interpretation:

- For \(0<T<1\), the circuit behaves as a current-to-voltage amplifier. Positive feedback **increases** both input and output resistance and increases the transresistance gain. This can be desirable for a high input-impedance current detector.
- As \(T\to1^{-}\), \(R_{\rm in}\) and the transresistance grow toward infinity; the circuit becomes very sensitive and may ring/oscillate because of parasitic capacitances.
- For \(T>1\), the small-signal input and output resistances become **negative**, and the linear operating point is unstable. The circuit then acts as a latch, Schmitt-like current threshold detector, or a negative-resistance element. If an inductor/capacitor is present at \(X\) or \(V_{\rm out}\), sustained oscillation is possible.
- In an actual saturated latch, the triode/cutoff regions, finite output resistances, and device leakage set the final states and switching thresholds.

---

### Summary
\[
\boxed{
\begin{minipage}{0.92\linewidth}
\(M_1\) is a common-source inverter. \(M_2\), with its drain at the input node \(X\) and gate at \(V_{\rm out}\), feeds the output back into the input as a current. The loop has two inversions, so it is a \textbf{positive-feedback current-input stage}. At small signal it presents
\[
R_{\rm in}=\frac{v_X}{i_{\rm in}}
=\frac{r_{o2}}{1-g_{m1}g_{m2}(R_{D1}\parallel r_{o1})r_{o2}},
\]
and a transresistance
\[
\frac{v_{\rm out}}{i_{\rm in}}
=-\frac{g_{m1}(R_{D1}\parallel r_{o1})r_{o2}}{1-T}.
\]
For \(T<1\) it is a high-input-impedance current-to-voltage amplifier whose input resistance is boosted by positive feedback. For \(T>1\), or when driven past its trip point, it exhibits negative resistance/hysteresis and can be used as a current-controlled latch, Schmitt trigger, or oscillator; it then requires a reset/discharge or careful compensation to return to the high-output state.
\end{minipage}
}
\]

If the input-current arrow is reversed, interchange the signs of \(I_{\rm in}\), \(V_X\), and the high/low-state polarities, but the positive-feedback nature remains the same.

- \(M_1\) is a common-source amplifier from \(X\) to \(V_{\rm out}\).
- \(M_2\) senses \(V_{\rm out}\) at its gate and returns a current to node \(X\).
- This is **shunt–shunt feedback** (current summing at the input, voltage sensing at the output), i.e. a current-to-voltage/transresistance stage.
- The loop is **positive feedback**:  
  \[
  V_X\uparrow \Rightarrow I_{D1}\uparrow \Rightarrow V_{\rm out}\downarrow
  \Rightarrow I_{D2}\downarrow
  \Rightarrow \text{less current is pulled from }X
  \Rightarrow V_X\uparrow .
  \]
  Thus the feedback reinforces the disturbance.

### Small-signal result
Let
\[
g_{m1},\,g_{m2}:\text{ transistor transconductances},\qquad
r_{o1},\,r_{o2}:\text{ output resistances},
\]
and define
\[
R_1=R_{D1}\parallel r_{o1}.
\]

Nodal equations are
\[
i_{\rm in}=\frac{v_X}{r_{o2}}+g_{m2}v_{\rm out},
\]
\[
0=\frac{v_{\rm out}}{R_{D1}}+\frac{v_{\rm out}}{r_{o1}}+g_{m1}v_X
  =\frac{v_{\rm out}}{R_1}+g_{m1}v_X .
\]
Hence
\[
v_{\rm out}=-g_{m1}R_1v_X,
\]
and the loop (return-ratio) magnitude is
\[
\boxed{T=g_{m1}g_{m2}R_1r_{o2}
      =g_{m1}g_{m2}(R_{D1}\parallel r_{o1})r_{o2}.}
\]

The input resistance seen at \(X\) is
\[
\boxed{R_{\rm in}=\frac{v_X}{i_{\rm in}}
       =\frac{r_{o2}}{1-T}.}
\]
The closed-loop current-to-voltage gain is
\[
\boxed{\frac{v_{\rm out}}{i_{\rm in}}
      =-\frac{g_{m1}R_1r_{o2}}{1-T}
      =-\frac{g_{m1}R_1r_{o2}}{1-g_{m1}g_{m2}R_1r_{o2}}.}
\]
With the ideal current source open-circuited for output-resistance calculation,
\[
\boxed{R_{\rm out}=\frac{R_1}{1-T}.}
\]

If the input current source has finite Norton resistance \(R_s\), replace \(r_{o2}\) in the loop gain by \(R_s\parallel r_{o2}\); instability occurs when the total conductance at \(X\),
\[
G_{\rm tot}\approx \frac{1}{R_s}+\frac{1}{r_{o2}}
       -g_{m1}g_{m2}R_1,
\]
becomes negative.

### Usual first-order approximation, neglecting channel-length modulation

\[
\boxed{R_{\rm in}\approx
-\frac{1}{g_{m1}g_{m2}R_{D1}}.}
\]
If \(r_{o1}\) is kept while \(r_{o2}\) is neglected,
\[
\boxed{R_{\rm in}\approx
-\frac{1}{g_{m1}g_{m2}(R_{D1}\parallel r_{o1})}.}
\]
In the high-loop-gain/strong-positive-feedback limit,
\[
\boxed{\frac{v_{\rm out}}{i_{\rm in}}\approx \frac{1}{g_{m2}},}
\]
with the sign depending on the chosen direction of \(I_{\rm in}\). For the arrow shown, a current injected into \(X\) ultimately produces a positive output change on the stable high-loop-gain branch.

### Meaning
- For \(T<1\), the feedback is positive but not strong enough to reverse the small-signal port resistance; \(R_{\rm in},R_{\rm out}>0\), although they are increased.
- At \(T=1\), \(R_{\rm in}\) and \(R_{\rm out}\) become infinite; the linearized circuit is at a boundary.
- For \(T>1\), both \(R_{\rm in}\) and \(R_{\rm out}\) become negative. This is the regenerative/negative-resistance regime. In the simple ideal model (\(r_o\to\infty\)), the positive feedback is effectively very strong and the circuit exhibits a negative input resistance

\]

\[
I_{\rm in}=I_{D2}=K_2(V_{\rm out}-V_T)^2,
\]
\[
I_{D1}=K_1(V_X-V_T)^2
      =\frac{V_{DD}-V_{\rm out}}{R_{D1}}.
\]
Thus, for a positive injected DC current,
\[
V_{\rm out}=V_T+\sqrt{\frac{I_{\rm in}}{K_2}},
\]
\[
V_X=V_T+\sqrt{\frac{V_{DD}-V_{\rm out}}{K_1R_{D1}}}.
\]

answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in Figure 22.

answer.text:
The circuit in Figure 22 is a **current-driven common-source stage with positive (regenerative) feedback**.

Assuming \(M_1\) and \(M_2\) are NMOS devices and the arrow of \(I_{\rm in}\) denotes current injected into node \(X\):

### 1. Feedback action
- \(M_1\) is a common-source inverter:  
  \[
  V_X\uparrow \;\Rightarrow\; I_{D1}\uparrow \;\Rightarrow\; V_{\rm out}\downarrow .
  \]
- \(M_2\) uses \(V_{\rm out}\) as its gate voltage and draws current from node \(X\):  
  \[
  V_{\rm out}\uparrow \;\Rightarrow\; I_{D2}\uparrow \;\Rightarrow\; V_X\!\downarrow .
  \]
- Combining these:  
  \[
  V_{\rm out}\uparrow \Rightarrow V_X\downarrow \Rightarrow V_{\rm out}\uparrow ,
  \]
  so the loop reinforces itself. The feedback is **positive/regenerative**. In feedback terminology it is a **shunt–shunt (voltage-sampled, current-mixed) positive-feedback loop**.

### 2. DC operation
Let
\[
K_i=\frac12\mu_n C_{\rm ox}\frac{W_i}{L_i}, \qquad
I_{Di}=K_i(V_{GSi}-V_{Ti})^2
\]
for saturation.

At the output node,
\[
I_{D1}=\frac{V_{DD}-V_{\rm out}}{R_{D1}}.
\]
At node \(X\), since the MOS gate draws no DC current,
\[
I_{D2}=I_{\rm in}
\]
for positive \(I_{\rm in}\) injected into \(X\).

If both devices are assumed in saturation, the static equations are
\[
K_1(V_X-V_{T1})^2=\frac{V_{DD}-V_{\rm out}}{R_{D1}},
\qquad
K_2(V_{\rm out}-V_{T2})^2=I_{\rm in}.
\]
Thus, in that idealized saturated region,
\[
V_{\rm out}\approx V_{T2}+\sqrt{\frac{I_{\rm in}}{K_2}},
\]
with saturation valid provided
\[
V_{\rm out}\ge V_X-V_{T1},
\qquad
V_X\ge V_{\rm out}-V_{T2}.
\]
When these inequalities fail, the triode expression must be used:
\[
I_D=K_i\!\left[2(V_{GS}-V_T)V_{DS}-V_{DS}^2\right].
\]

In practice, the stable states are usually:
- **Output high:** \(V_{\rm out}\approx V_{DD}\), \(M_1\) off/weak, \(M_2\) in triode sinking the input current.
- **Output low:** \(M_1\) on, \(M_2\) off or weak; positive feedback holds this state after triggering.

Because of the positive feedback, the transfer from \(I_{\rm in}\) to \(V_{\rm out}\) is regenerative. Increasing current into \(X\) eventually turns \(M_1\) on and causes a rapid switch to the low-output state; removing or reversing the current can cause the opposite transition. The two switching thresholds are generally different, giving **hysteresis**. With an ideal zero-current source, the state can be held by charge on the gate node; the circuit therefore behaves like a **current-controlled latch/Schmitt trigger**. If the current-source polarity is opposite, reverse the sign of \(I_{\rm in}\).

### 3. Small-signal behavior
Define
\[
g_{mi}=\frac{\partial I_{Di}}{\partial V_{GSi}},\qquad
g_{ds2}=\frac{\partial I_{D2}}{\partial V_{DS2}},
\]
and
\[
R_{o1}=R_{D1}\parallel r_{o1}.
\]
At a presumed bias point,
\[
v_{\rm out}=-g_{m1}R_{o1}v_X,
\]
and, with current \(i_{\rm in}\) injected into \(X\),
\[
i_{\rm in}=g_{ds2}v_X+g_{m2}v_{\rm out}.
\]
Therefore the small-signal input resistance seen at \(X\) is
\[
\boxed{
R_{\rm in,X}
=
\frac{v_X}{i_{\rm in}}
=
\frac{1}{g_{ds2}-g_{m1}g_{m2}R_{o1}}
}
\]
and the transresistance is
\[
\boxed{
\frac{v_{\rm out}}{i_{\rm in}}
=
-\frac{g_{m1}R_{o1}}
{g_{ds2}-g_{m1}g_{m2}R_{o1}}
}.
\]
The positive-feedback loop transmission is approximately
\[
T\simeq \frac{g_{m1}g_{m2}R_{o1}}{g_{ds2}}.
\]
- If \(T<1\), the operating point can be stable; positive feedback increases the effective input resistance.
- If \(T>1\), the denominator in \(R_{\rm in,X}\) becomes negative, so the input presents a **negative resistance**. Any capacitance at \(X\) then forms a right-half-plane pole; the circuit will leave the linear region and latch or, with additional poles, may oscillate.
- At the switching threshold,
  \[
  g_{m1}g_{m2}R_{o1}\approx g_{ds2}.
  \]

### Summary
Figure 22 is a **current-input, voltage-output positive-feedback stage**. \(M_1\) provides the inverting gain and \(M_2\) feeds the output voltage back as a current to the high-impedance input node \(X\). It exhibits regeneration, negative input resistance in the active region when loop gain exceeds unity, and hysteresis/bistability in the large-signal sense. It is therefore useful as a **latch, regenerative comparator, Schmitt trigger, or negative-resistance element**, but not as an ordinary linear amplifier unless the loop gain is kept below unity.

\[
v_i=V_{S1},\qquad v_X=V_{D1}=V_{G2},\qquad v_o=V_{\rm out},
\]

and take \(i_{\rm in}\) positive in the arrow direction, i.e. into the input/source node of \(M_1\).

- \(M_1\) is a common-gate input stage; its source is the low-impedance input (summing) node.
- \(M_2\) is a common-source voltage-gain/inverting stage.
- \(R_F\) connects the output back to the input node. The output voltage is sampled in parallel (shunt) and a feedback current is returned in parallel to the input:
  \[
  \boxed{\text{shunt–shunt (voltage-shunt) negative feedback.}}
  \]
- The overall amplifier is a transimpedance (current-to-voltage) amplifier. A positive \(i_{\rm in}\) raises the source of \(M_1\), raises \(v_X\), and therefore lowers \(v_o\); thus the transresistance is negative for the indicated current direction.

\[
g_{o1}=\frac1{r_{o1}},\quad g_{o2}=\frac1{r_{o2}},
\quad G_{D1}=\frac1{R_{D1}},\quad G_{D2}=\frac1{R_{D2}},
\quad G_F=\frac1{R_F}.
\]

\[
A_X\equiv \frac{v_X}{v_i}
=
\frac{g_{m1}+g_{o1}}{G_{D1}+g_{o1}}
\approx g_{m1}R_{D1},
\]

and the small-signal input resistance at the source of \(M_1\), with the feedback removed, is

\[
R_{i0}
=
\frac{R_{D1}+r_{o1}}{1+g_{m1}r_{o1}}
\approx \frac1{g_{m1}}.
\]

Let

\[
G_i=\frac1{R_{i0}},\qquad
g_X=g_{m2}A_X
=
g_{m2}\frac{g_{m1}+g_{o1}}{G_{D1}+g_{o1}},
\qquad
G_{o0}=G_{D2}+g_{o2}
=
\frac1{R_{D2}\parallel r_{o2}}.
\]

The exact mid-band small-signal results (within this MOS model) are

\[
\boxed{
\frac{v_o}{i_{\rm in}}
=
-\frac{g_X-G_F}
{G_i(G_{o0}+G_F)+G_F(G_{o0}+g_X)}
}
\]

\[
\boxed{
R_{\rm in,cl}
=
\left[
G_i+G_F\frac{G_{o0}+g_X}{G_{o0}+G_F}
\right]^{-1}
}
\]

\[
\boxed{
R_{\rm out,cl}
=
\left[
G_{o0}+G_F+
\frac{(g_X-G_F)G_F}{G_i+G_F}
\right]^{-1}

\frac{v_o}{i_{\rm in}}
=
-\frac{g_{m1}g_{m2}R_{D1}-\frac1{R_F}}
{g_{m1}\left(\frac1{R_{D2}}+\frac1{R_F}\right)
+\frac1{R_F}\left(\frac1{R_{D2}}+g_{m1}g_{m2}R_{D1}\right)}
}
\]

for negligible body effect.

\[
R_{m,\rm OL}
=
\frac{v_o}{i_{\rm in}}\bigg|_{R_F\to\infty}
\approx
-g_{m2}R_{D1}(R_{D2}\parallel r_{o2})

\[

\]

\[
\beta\approx \frac1{R_F},
\]

\[

L\approx
\frac{g_{m2}R_{D1}(R_{D2}\parallel r_{o2})}{R_F}

{1+L}

\[
\boxed{
R_{\rm in,cl}\approx \frac{R_{i0}}{1+L}
\approx \frac{1/g_{m1}}{1+L}
}
\]

\[
\boxed{
R_{\rm out,cl}\approx
\frac{R_{D2}\parallel r_{o2}}{1+L}
}
\]

For large loop gain \(L\gg1\),

\[
\boxed{

}
\]

which is the ideal transimpedance-amplifier result. In that limit the input node is a virtual ground, and the current through \(R_F\) in the direction drawn in the figure is

- For \(M_1\):
  \[

answer.text:
Assume the two devices are n-channel MOSFETs and are biased in saturation. The circuit is a two-stage CMOS **shunt–shunt (voltage-shunt) negative-feedback transimpedance amplifier**.

- \(M_1\) is a common-gate input stage whose source is the current-input node.
- \(M_2\) is a common-source inverting second stage.
- \(R_{D1},R_{D2}\) are the load resistors and \(V_b\) biases \(M_1\).
- \(R_F\) feeds the output voltage back to the input as a current; this is negative feedback.
- For high loop gain, the input node is a virtual ground and all signal current flows through \(R_F\):
  \[
  V_{\rm out}\approx -I_{\rm in}R_F.
  \]
  The output is inverted relative to a positive current injected into the input node. The current \(i_{RF}\) shown from output to input is approximately \(i_{RF}\approx -I_{\rm in}\).

### Low-frequency small-signal result

Define
\[
G_{D1}=\frac1{R_{D1}},\quad G_{D2}=\frac1{R_{D2}},\quad
G_F=\frac1{R_F},
\]
\[
g_{m1}'=g_{m1}+g_{mb1}
\]
(use \(g_{mb1}=0\) if the body is tied to the source),
\[
g_{o1}=\frac1{r_{o1}},\qquad g_{o2}=\frac1{r_{o2}}.
\]
The voltage gain from the input node to the drain of \(M_1\) is
\[
A_1=\frac{v_x}{v_s}
   =\frac{g_{m1}'+g_{o1}}{G_{D1}+g_{o1}},
\]
the conductance seen at the input node is
\[
g_s=G_{D1}A_1
   =\frac{G_{D1}(g_{m1}'+g_{o1})}{G_{D1}+g_{o1}},
\]
and at the output node
\[
g_o=G_{D2}+g_{o2}
\]
(add any external load conductance if present). Also define
\[
G_m=g_{m2}A_1.
\]

The small-signal nodal equations are
\[
I_{\rm in}=(g_s+G_F)v_s-G_Fv_o,
\]
\[
0=(G_m-G_F)v_s+(g_o+G_F)v_o.
\]
Hence the transimpedance is
\[
\boxed{
Z_T=\frac{v_o}{I_{\rm in}}
=
\frac{G_F-G_m}
{g_sg_o+G_F(g_s+g_o+G_m)}
}
\]
with \(I_{\rm in}\) entering the input node. The input and output small-signal resistances are
\[
\boxed{
R_{\rm in}=\frac{v_s}{I_{\rm in}}
=
\frac{g_o+G_F}
{g_sg_o+G_F(g_s+g_o+G_m)}
}
\]
and, with the input current source opened,
\[
\boxed{
R_{\rm out}=
\frac{g_s+G_F}
{g_sg_o+G_F(g_s+g_o+G_m)}.
}
\]
These are the exact low-frequency results under the above model.

If channel-length modulation and body effect are neglected,
\[
g_s=g_{m1},\qquad g_o=\frac1{R_{D2}},\qquad
G_m=g_{m1}g_{m2}R_{D1},
\]
so
\[
Z_T=
\frac{\frac1{R_F}-g_{m1}g_{m2}R_{D1}}
{\frac{g_{m1}}{R_{D2}}
+\frac1{R_F}\left(g_{m1}+\frac1{R_{D2}}
+g_{m1}g_{m2}R_{D1}\right)}.
\]
The open-loop transimpedance (\(R_F\to\infty\)) is approximately
\[
Z_{T,\rm ol}\approx
-g_{m2}R_{D1}(R_{D2}\parallel r_{o2}),
\]
while the dominant loop gain is
\[
L\approx
\frac{g_{m2}R_{D1}(R_{D2}\parallel r_{o2})}{R_F}.
\]
For \(L\gg1\),
\[
Z_T\approx -R_F,
\qquad
R_{\rm in}\ll R_{\rm in,ol},
\qquad
R_{\rm out}\ll R_{\rm out,ol}.
\]
A common approximate expression, ignoring loading by \(R_F\), is
\[
Z_T\approx
-\frac{A_oR_F}{A_o+R_F},
\qquad
A_o=g_{m2}R_{D1}(R_{D2}\parallel r_{o2}).
\]

### Frequency behavior
With device and load capacitances, replace the conductances in the nodal equations by \(G+sC\). The circuit normally has a second-order response. Using a dominant output pole,
\[
\omega_{-3\rm dB}\approx (1+L)\frac1{(R_{D2}\parallel r_{o2})C_{\rm out}},
\]
so negative feedback increases bandwidth as it lowers the closed-loop transimpedance. However, the two high-impedance nodes at the drain of \(M_1\) and the output can produce peaking or oscillation for some \(R_F\), so phase margin must be checked. The common-gate \(M_1\) gives a low input impedance and isolates input capacitance, which is the main reason this topology is useful in broadband transimpedance amplifiers.

### Bias/saturation requirements
For proper operation,
\[
V_b-V_S>V_{TH1},\qquad
V_X\gtrsim V_b-V_{TH1},
\]
\[
V_X>V_{TH2},\qquad
V_O\gtrsim V_X-V_{TH2},
\]
where \(V_S\) is the dc input-node voltage, \(X\) is the drain of \(M_1\), and \(O\) is the output. The bias currents satisfy approximately
\[
I_{D1}=\frac{V_{DD}-V_X}{R_{D1}},
\]
\[
\frac{V_{DD}-V_O}{R_{D2}}
=I_{D2}+\frac{V_O-V_S}{R_F},
\]
with the input-node dc KCL including any dc component of \(I_{\rm in}\).

In short, the circuit is a negative-feedback CMOS transimpedance amplifier: \(R_F\) sets \(V_{\rm out}/I_{\rm in}\approx -R_F\), the common-gate stage lowers the input resistance, and the feedback lowers both input and output resistance while improving bandwidth and linearity.
